Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images California Controversial California oil pipeline can continue to operate, judge rules State sought to stop system off coast of Santa Barbara from resuming operations after Trump ordered its reopening Dani Anguiano Thu 20 Aug 2026 20.13 EDT First published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 16.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A controversial oil pipeline can continue to operate off the California coast after a judge gave it the green light this week, despite the opposition of state regulators and environmental groups. The system off the coast of Santa Barbara resumed operations earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade after Donald Trump ordered Sable Offshore Corporation to reopen it, citing US energy needs during the war in Iran. It had been closed since 2015 when a burst pipe caused one of California’s worst oil spills, and its reopening was supposed to be governed by a federal consent decree. For months, California has sought to stop Sable from moving oil through pipelines, describing the company’s actions as an “egregious trespass on public land” that would cause irreparable harm. The Trump administration invoked the Defense Production Act (DPA) , which grants the president authority over industries in the interest of national defense, and the company said the directive from the federal government superseded the orders of state regulators. This week, Judge Stephen Wilson ruled that the pipelines can remain in operation and shifted oversight to federal authorities. “Finally, as the court has now discussed, the DPA order does, as a matter of law, pre-empt the enforcement of any state law that conflicts with Sable’s ability to operate the onshore pipeline, including the trespass claim,” Wilson wrote in his ruling. In the ruling, Wilson also fined Sable $1.5m for violating the consent decree without authorization and approval from a state agency or petitioning the court on the matter. Sable bought the pipeline from ExxonMobile in 2024 and for more than a year was seeking to restart offshore oil production. In March, the Trump administration invoked the emergency powers of the DPA to order the company “restore operation” to address “supply disruption risks” that it said were caused by California policies. Chris Wright, the US energy secretary, argued it would improve the US oil supply and restore a system “vital to our national security and defense”. “The Trump administration remains committed to putting all Americans and their energy security first,” Wright said. “Unfortunately, some state leaders have not adhered to those same principles, with potentially disastrous consequences not just for their residents, but also our national security.” Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, said Trump’s moves in the Middle East had caused gas prices to surge and that he was “using this crisis of his own making to attempt what he’s wanted to do for years: open California’s coast for his oil industry friends so they can poison our beaches”. A spokesperson for the California department of justice said the state was “reviewing all of our legal options”. They said: “The Trump administration continues to allow Sable to profit at the expense of our environment and public health. California will continue to fight back against attempts to interfere with our sovereign authority.” The matter has been working its way through the courts for months. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief reporting from Budapest, Hungary BUDAPEST, HUNGARY ( Worthy News ) – Hungary’s new government of Prime Minister Péter Magyar was racing Sunday to complete rule-of-law and anti-corruption reforms ahead of a crucial Monday deadline that could unlock 10 billion euros ($11.7 billion) in European Union recovery funding blocked during the Viktor Orbán era. The August 31 deadline provides an early test of Magyar’s pledge to repair Budapest’s strained relationship with Brussels and restore access to billions of euros in European funding after his landslide election victory ended Orbán’s 16 years in power. Hungary must complete reforms and investments under its revised Recovery and Resilience Plan by Monday to remain eligible for the funding, comprising about 6.5 billion euros in grants and 3.5 billion euros in preferential loans. Start your day with Christian news and biblical encouragement from Worthy News. The government is seeking to satisfy 27 so-called “super milestones” established by the European Commission, the European Union’s executive. They include 21 related to fighting corruption and improving transparency, four concerning judicial independence and two involving audits of EU spending. BILLIONS AT STAKE “We are making good progress in meeting the milestones related to recovery funds: we have already fulfilled two-thirds of our commitments, and the settlement of the remaining cases is in its final stage,” said a spokesperson for Hungary’s Ministry of Transport and Investment, which oversees EU funds. The ministry added that it considered fulfillment of all the remaining milestones realistic, stressing that the government wanted to “bring home every euro cent due to Hungary.” Magyar hopes the measures will help end years of tensions between Budapest and Brussels over corruption, judicial independence, public procurement and other rule-of-law concerns that marked the government of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. His cabinet has moved to strengthen anti-corruption safeguards and judicial independence while pursuing Hungary’s accession to the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, which investigates crimes involving EU money. EU FUNDING DECISION EU finance ministers approved Hungary’s revised recovery plan in July, but payments remain conditional on the European Commission determining that Budapest has satisfactorily completed the required milestones and targets. The deadline follows a political agreement reached earlier this year between Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen aimed at restoring Hungary’s access to European funding after years of confrontation under Orbán. Magyar has made recovering the money a central promise of his new government, arguing that Hungary lost access to billions of euros largely because of corruption and rule-of-law problems under his predecessor. Yet as officials in Budapest raced to satisfy Brussels, the rising Danube was providing some welcome relief elsewhere in Hungary. DANUBE BRINGS RELIEF The country’s only nuclear power station, at Paks south of Budapest, returned to full capacity last week after record-low water levels in the Danube had brought the plant close to its first complete shutdown in more than four decades. All four reactors and eight turbines were operating again after weeks of severely reduced production, Magyar said, with the plant reaching its maximum output of about 2,000 megawatts. The Paks facility, which produces nearly half of Hungary’s electricity, relies on the Danube for cooling and fell to a fraction of normal production during the summer drought. Rising river levels and emergency engineering measures near the plant helped restore operations. Authorities constructed an underwater barrier to raise the Danube around the cooling-water intake after extraordinarily low levels threatened electricity supplies. SWIMMERS TAKE TO DANUBE The recovering river was also attracting attention for a rather different reason this weekend as nearly 1,000 people plunged into the Danube in central Budapest for the first organized crossing of its kind in six years. Authorities closed one of the normally busy stretches of the river to shipping for four hours Saturday as participants swam between Corvinus University and the Budapest University of Technology and Economics. Nearly 40 paramedics and 12 motorboats watched over the swimmers during the Generali OWT Danube Crossing, organizers said. One British participant living in Budapest described the swim as “a fantastic experience,” adding: “Every Budapest resident should try it once.” Organizers said the water was clean and the route safe, despite longstanding concerns among some Hungarians about swimming in the river. https://www.politico.eu/article/alan-mil.text: LIVERPOOL, England — Chancellor John Healey doesn’t have the cash to scrap employer national insurance contributions for young people, the U.K. government’s youth employment adviser Alan Milburn said Tuesday. Speaking in the POLITICO pub at the Labour Party conference, the former Cabinet minister rejected a call from MPs on parliament’s work and pensions committee to cut employer national insurance contributions for under 25s in a bid to tackle mass youth unemployment. “The problem is it’ll cost you £5.1 billion,” Milburn said when asked about the proposal to cut the tax on earnings paid by workers and employers. “If somebody’s got £5.1 billion pounds, it isn’t John Healey, so we’ve got a problem.” It would “not be an effective use of public money” because of the “deadweight cost,” he added. Advertisement Advertisement Milburn — who published a report in May warning the number of young people not in work or education could hit 1.25 million by the early 2030s without urgent action — is currently drawing up recommendations for ministers to address the crisis. “In six months time, this is going to feel much more like a manifesto for change,” he said. The former health secretary — who was chair of the Social Mobility Commission between 2012 and 2017 — also warned that young people from working class backgrounds face greater barriers to opportunity today. Reflecting on his own journey from growing up on a council estate to sitting around the Cabinet table, Milburn said he has reached the “pretty depressing conclusion” that it seems “less likely rather than more likely” to happen today. “It is one of the reasons why we’ve got to deal with this challenge,” he said. “Life shouldn’t have to rely on luck; it should rely on opportunity.”

Russia: Soldier killed in car explosion in Saint Petersburg Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 12 November 2026 - 15:57 GMT+1 A Russian serviceman was killed when his car exploded in Saint Petersburg on Thursday. Investigators have opened a murder inquiry, while local media report that another person was injured. … More The explosion occurred at about 7 am in the Shushary area of the city's Pushkinsky district, on Kolpino Highway, leaving the vehicle badly damaged. A passing bus also had its windows shattered by the blast. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Russian news outlet Fontanka reported that the victim was a colonel serving as chief navigator of the 6th Air and Air Defence Army . According to the outlet, an explosive device attached beneath his vehicle was remotely detonated as he drove away. Fontanka reported that a family member nearby had been also hurt . Russian authorities have not officially identified the serviceman or confirmed the cause of the explosion. The Investigative Committee has opened a murder investigation , with forensic experts examining the scene. The blast comes more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Several Russian military officials have since been killed in attacks on Russian territory , some of which have been attributed to Kyiv, although Ukrainian authorities rarely claim responsibility. Investigators have not established any connection between Thursday's explosion and the war .
